haiku-low.q1: Pages of 500 live products, ordered by id ascending, each requested after the last id. Fetched one at a time, never in parallel.
haiku-low.q2: Stored in the sync_state row as the cursor, the id of the last saved product, written in the same transaction as the page's rows, so position never outruns data.
haiku-low.q3: Step 3 catch-up replays every change since start_seq, including deletes, into staging before the swap, under the newer-wins rule.
haiku-low.q4: Server returns 410 "resync required". The device runs a resync, starting a new full download while keeping the old catalogue until swap.
haiku-low.q5: Staging is emptied and refilled by a new full download and catch-up. One transaction swaps it into products; reps see it then.
haiku-low.q6: Launch or returning to foreground triggers it. At most once per 15 minutes, using last_incremental_started_at, and never during a full download.
haiku-low.q7: Retry the same request after waits of 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, five attempts in total. Then stop and keep saved data.
haiku-low.q8: The page in progress finishes and saves; the download pauses and resumes when Wi-Fi returns.
haiku-low.q9: Applied only if its change_seq is higher than the device's stored change_seq for that product; otherwise ignored.
haiku-low.q10: Starts from last_seq, the change_seq of the last applied change, saved with each page's rows in the same transaction.
haiku-low.q11: Not stated what it reads. Deletes are included as tombstone rows marked deleted, kept 7 days, in change_seq order.

sonnet.q1: Keyset pagination: pages of 500 live products ordered by id ascending, each request using after_id = saved cursor. Pages are fetched one at a time, never in parallel.
sonnet.q2: In the single sync_state row in SQLite (the cursor, the id of the last product of the last saved page). Each saved page writes its rows and its new cursor in one transaction, so the cursor never runs ahead of the saved data.
sonnet.q3: The server returns start_seq at the start. After the pages are downloaded, the device runs a catch-up from start_seq via GET /catalogue/changes (up to 1,000 per request, repeated while full), applying changes to staging under the newer-wins rule. The swap happens only after the catch-up ends. Changes after the last catch-up request are fetched by the first incremental sync after the swap, which starts from last_seq.
sonnet.q4: The server answers HTTP 410 'resync required'. The device then goes to step 6 (resync): it keeps the old products, empties staging, clears cursor and last_seq, and starts a new full download (Wi-Fi only).
sonnet.q5: It is built in the separate products_staging table (emptied first), filled by the page download and catch-up. The app's browsing screens read only products. In one SQLite transaction the swap replaces all products rows with the staging rows, empties staging and sets download_state to complete, and from then on reps see the new catalogue. The old catalogue stays visible until then.
sonnet.q6: App launch or the app returning to the foreground. It runs at most once every 15 minutes (skipped if last_incremental_started_at is less than 15 minutes ago), and not while a full download is in progress.
sonnet.q7: It retries the same request: wait 2 s before the first retry, doubling each time (2, 4, 8, 16 s), at most 5 attempts in total. After the fifth failure it stops, keeps everything already saved, and waits for the next trigger.
sonnet.q8: If the device drops to cellular, the page in progress finishes and is saved, then the download pauses and resumes when Wi-Fi returns. The network is checked before each page.
sonnet.q9: By the newer-wins rule: the row or delete is applied only if its change_seq is higher than the change_seq the device already holds for that product. Otherwise it is ignored.
sonnet.q10: It starts from last_seq (GET /catalogue/changes?since=<last_seq>). last_seq moves forward with each page of changes, saved in the same transaction as that page's rows (set to the change_seq of the last change applied).
sonnet.q11: NOT STATED for what the server reads to build the feed. The document says only that changes come from change_seq, a single ever-increasing counter stamped on every insert, update or delete, and the feed is returned in change_seq order. Deletes are included as changes. They are kept as tombstones (rows marked deleted) for 7 days, then purged.
